result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.second_order_centrality()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Compute the second order centrality for nodes in the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L14253-L14426){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.second_order_centrality( attr_name=None, return_dict=False, ) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} Second order centrality measures the standard deviation of return times to a node in a perpetual random walk on the graph. Lower values indicate higher centrality, as nodes with lower return time variance are more centrally positioned in the network structure. This metric is particularly useful for identifying nodes that are consistently reached in random walks, indicating their importance in network flow and connectivity patterns. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of node attribute to store centrality values. If `None`, uses `second_order_centrality`. Only used when `return_dict=False`. [return_dict]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns dict mapping node IDs to centrality values. If `False`, stores values in graph and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [dict or Graph]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_dict=True`: dictionary mapping node ID to centrality value. If `return_dict=False`: self (for method chaining). ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If either: (1) the graph is directed (algorithm only works for undirected graphs), (2) the graph is empty, or (3) the graph is not connected. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} **Algorithm Overview:** The algorithm implements the analytical solution from Kermarrec et al. (2011) based on Metropolis-Hastings random walks: 1. Balance the graph by adding self-loops to equalize in-degrees 2. Create transition probability matrix `P` 3. For each node `i`, solve the linear system: `(I - Q_i) * M[:, i] = 1` where `Q_i` is `P` with column `i` zeroed 4. Compute centrality as: `sqrt(2 * sum(M[:, i]) - n * (n + 1))` **Complexity:** - Time: `O(n³)` due to solving `n` linear systems of size `n×n` - Space: `O(n²)` for storing matrices **Interpretation:** - **Lower values** = **higher centrality** (more central nodes) - Values represent consistency of return times in random walks - Captures both direct and indirect influence through network structure - Complements first-order metrics like degree or betweenness **Current Limitation:** - Only supports unweighted graphs (all edges treated equally) ## Examples {.doc-examples} Identify central nodes in a path graph (lower values = higher centrality): ::: {#f02f7eea .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec # Create a simple path: 0 - 1 - 2 - 3 - 4 graph = ec.Graph() for i in range(5): graph.add_node(label=str(i)) for i in range(4): graph.add_edge(str(i), str(i+1)) soc = graph.second_order_centrality(return_dict=True) # Keys are node IDs, not labels -- map back to see which node is most central most_central_id = min(soc, key=soc.get) graph.get_label_from_id(most_central_id) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` '2' ``` ::: ::: The middle of the path has the lowest (and therefore most central) value: ::: {#887adf4c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} soc[most_central_id] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 4.47213595499958 ``` ::: ::: Compare centrality across different graph structures -- a star's center is far more central than any leaf: ::: {#2a675e7f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} star = ec.Graph() star.add_node(label='center') for i in range(5): star.add_node(label=f'leaf_{i}') star.add_edge('center', f'leaf_{i}') star_soc = star.second_order_centrality(return_dict=True) center_id = star.get_id_from_label('center') leaf_id = star.get_id_from_label('leaf_0') star_soc[center_id], star_soc[leaf_id] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` (4.472135954999581, 16.124515496597105) ``` ::: ::: In a complete graph, every node is structurally identical, so all centrality values come out equal: ::: {#bf0b9d10 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} complete = ec.Graph() for i in range(4): complete.add_node(label=str(i)) for i in range(4): for j in range(i+1, 4): complete.add_edge(str(i), str(j)) complete_soc = complete.second_order_centrality(return_dict=True) vals = list(complete_soc.values()) all(abs(v - vals[0]) < 0.01 for v in vals) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` True ``` ::: ::: Storing centrality as a node attribute makes it available for later analysis without recomputing: ::: {#61cc1416 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ( ec.Graph() .add_node(label='A') .add_node(label='B') .add_node(label='C') .add_node(label='D') .add_edge('A', 'B') .add_edge('B', 'C') .add_edge('C', 'D') ) graph.second_order_centrality(attr_name='soc') graph.get_node_attrs('soc') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` {3: 3.4641016151377544, 1: 6.6332495807108, 4: 6.6332495807108, 2: 3.4641016151377544} ``` ::: :::
